Sample text:
---
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are apologies that felt too small for the thing they were apologizing for. Some are declarations that felt too large for the person receiving them. One is just the word "hey" typed seventeen times, each version deleted, each version somehow worse than the last.

My grandmother used to say that some things are better left unsaid, and I used to believe her. Now I think she was wrong, or at least incomplete. Some things are better left *said badly* than left unsaid entirely. The silence becomes its own message. It calcifies. It becomes the thing you both pretend isn't there while it grows teeth.

I think about this when I'm lying in bed at 2 AM, thumb hovering over the send button, composing a message to someone I haven't spoken to in three years. The message would be honest. It would explain why I disappeared. It would take responsibility for the specific ways I failed them. It would ask for nothing, demand nothing, offer only the truth of what happened and why I was afraid.

I don't send it. I never send it. Instead I delete it, and then I type it again the next night, and the cycle continues until the words lose their meaning, until "I'm sorry" becomes just shapes on a screen, until I can't remember what I was sorry for.

There's a particular loneliness to this. Not the loneliness of being alone, which is honest and clean. The loneliness of being *almost* connected. Of having the door open, the light on, the phone in your hand, and still choosing the dark.

I wonder sometimes if the people I've lost would even want to hear from me. Maybe the silence is kinder. Maybe my apology would just reopen a wound they've finally learned to live with. Maybe I'm not trying to make amends. Maybe I'm just trying to make myself feel better, and the difference matters.

But then I remember the letter I found last year, written by my grandfather to my grandmother in 1962, the year before they married. He was in Korea. She was in Ohio. The letter was four pages long and he apologized for something small—a missed phone call, a harsh word—and he wrote about the way the light looked through the tent flap at dawn, and he wrote "I am thinking of you constantly" seventeen times, and I realized that love is mostly this. Love is the willingness to be ridiculous. To say the thing that makes you vulnerable. To send the message even when you're afraid of the answer.

He kept the letter. She kept it too, in a box with his medals and a lock of her hair from when she was nineteen. They were married for fifty-one years. I don't know if the letter saved anything, or started anything, or was just one small brick in a wall they built together. But I know they chose to keep it. They chose to remember that someone had once thought of them constantly, had once written it down, had once been brave enough to send it.

I'm trying to be braver. I'm trying to send the messages. Most of them still go unsent, but some get through. A text to my sister at midnight: "I love you, I'm proud of you, I'm sorry I'm not better at showing up." A voice memo to an old friend: "I miss you. I don't know how to fix it. I just wanted you to know." These are small things. They don't fix anything. But they're real, and they're mine, and they're out in the world now instead of trapped in the graveyard of my drafts.

The folder is smaller now. Forty-seven became forty-three became thirty-nine. Some messages I finally sent. Some I deleted for good, recognizing that the urge to speak was really just an urge to be heard, and that being heard by the wrong person, or in the wrong way, or at the wrong time, can be worse than silence.

I still have the "hey" that I typed seventeen times. I keep it as a reminder. Not of failure, but of the effort. Of the fact that I was trying, even when I didn't know how. Even when the words kept coming out wrong.

There's a Buddhist concept I read about once: the idea that we are all Buddhas, but we don't know it. We walk around with our enlightenment hidden, our wisdom buried, our capacity for compassion locked behind fear and habit and the stories we tell ourselves about who we are and what we deserve.

I think about this when I'm afraid to send the message. When I tell myself that I'm not worth the response, or that the other person is better off without me, or that love is a finite resource and I've already spent my share. These are stories. They're not true. They're just familiar, and familiarity feels like safety, even when it's really just a cage with the door left open.

The door is open. The light is on. The phone is in my hand.

I'm going to send something tonight. Something small. Something true. Something that might not matter to anyone but me, but that I need to put into the world before I forget how.

The weight of unsent messages is the weight of a life half-lived. I'm tired of carrying it. I'm tired of being afraid.

Hey. I'm still here. I'm sorry I disappeared. I'm trying to do better. I hope you are too.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A first-person meditation turns the recurring image of unsent texts into a personal story about regret, fear, and small acts of reconnection.

## Grounded reading
The voice is intimate and self-questioning, moving between the immediate scene of a phone held at night and inherited memories of love expressed in letters. Its pathos comes from wanting to make amends while doubting whether an apology would serve the other person or merely ease the speaker’s own guilt. The ending offers the reader a modest invitation: not that every message should be sent, but that a small, imperfect truth can be worth putting into the world.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample centers drafts, the hovering send button, family letters, and the difference between speaking to connect and speaking to be heard. It emphasizes vulnerability and responsibility over grand reconciliation: some messages are sent, some deleted, and neither choice is treated as simple. The repeated door, light, and phone imagery gives fear a physical shape, while the final “Hey” makes the desired courage small and concrete.

## Evidence line
> The silence becomes its own message.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the piece is coherent and distinctive in its recurring images and balanced treatment of apology, self-interest, and connection, though its reflective arc is also tightly shaped around one central metaphor.
